column2: Time, inherent nature, necessity, chance, the elements, the womb, the person — are these to be considered the cause? Not a mere combination of them, because of the existence of the Self; and even the Self is powerless over the cause of pleasure and pain.
Those who followed the path of meditation and yoga saw the divine power of the Self, hidden by its own qualities. He is the One who presides over all those causes, from Time to the Self.

We contemplate Him as a wheel with one rim, threefold, with sixteen ends, fifty spokes, twenty counter-spokes, six sets of eight, one rope of many forms, three different paths, and one delusion arising from two causes.

We contemplate Him as a river of five streams, from five sources, fierce and crooked, with the five breaths as its waves, with the fivefold perception as its source, with five whirlpools, rushing with a flood of five sorrows, divided into fifty kinds, and having five branches.
In this vast wheel of Brahman, in which all live and all rest, the swan wanders about, thinking of itself and the Impeller as different. Accepted by Him, it then attains immortality.

This has been sung as the supreme Brahman: in it the triad is firmly established, and the Imperishable. Knowers of Brahman, having known what lies within it, are absorbed in Brahman, devoted to it, and freed from birth.

The Lord supports this whole united together — the perishable and the imperishable, the manifest and the unmanifest. The Self, not being lord, is bound through being an enjoyer; knowing the God, it is freed from all fetters.

There are two unborn ones — the knowing and the unknowing, the lord and the one who is not lord — and one unborn female, connected with the enjoyer and the enjoyed. The Self is infinite, of universal form, and not a doer. When one finds this triad, that is Brahman.

The perishable is Pradhana; the immortal and imperishable is Hara. The One God rules over both the perishable and the Self. By meditating on Him, uniting with Him, and becoming one in being with Him, one finally attains the cessation of all illusion.

By knowing God, all fetters fall away; with afflictions destroyed, birth and death cease. By meditating on Him, at the dissolution of the body, one attains the third state — lordship over all; alone, with all desires fulfilled.

This, which abides in the Self, is to be known as eternal; beyond this there is nothing further to be known. Having recognised the enjoyer, the enjoyed and the Impeller, everything has been declared: this threefold is Brahman.

As the form of fire lodged in its source is not seen, yet its subtle essence is not destroyed, and it is grasped again and again in the fuel that is its source — so, in the body, both are grasped by means of the syllable Om.
Making one's own body the lower fire-stick and Om the upper fire-stick, by the practice of the friction of meditation one will see the God, hidden as it were.
As oil in sesame seeds, butter in curds, water in stream beds, and fire in fire-sticks, so the Self is grasped in the self by one who looks upon it with truthfulness and austerity.
The Self, pervading all, like butter contained in milk, is rooted in self-knowledge and austerity — that is the supreme teaching of Brahman.
Yoking the mind first, for the sake of truth, Savitr, having discerned the light of fire, brought it forth from the earth.
With mind yoked, we are under the impulse of the divine Savitr, that with our strength we may attain heaven.
Having yoked the gods with mind, going to heaven with insight, may Savitr impel them to make a great light.
The wise yoke the mind and yoke their thoughts, the priests of the great and wise priest. The One who knows the rites has assigned the offices; great is the praise of the divine Savitr.
I yoke your ancient Brahman with homage; let the praise go forth like the path of the sun. Let all the sons of the immortal hear, who have reached the divine abodes.
Where fire is churned, where the wind is restrained, where the soma overflows — there the mind is born.
Impelled by Savitr, delight in the ancient Brahman; there, where you make your abode, your offering does not fail.
Holding the body steady with the three parts erect, and drawing the senses with the mind into the heart, the wise man should cross all the fearful streams by the boat of Brahman.

In a level and clean place, free from pebbles, fire and sand, favourable to the mind by the sound of water and the like, not offensive to the eye, in a cave sheltered from the wind — there let him practise.
Fog, smoke, sun, wind, fire, fireflies, lightning, crystal and moon — these are the forms that come first, making Brahman manifest in yoga.

When earth, water, fire, air and space have arisen and the fivefold quality of yoga has come into play, there is no disease, no old age, no death for one who has obtained a body made of the fire of yoga.
Lightness, health, freedom from craving, clarity of complexion, a pleasant voice, a pleasant smell, and little excretion — these, they say, are the first signs of progress in yoga.
As a disc of metal smeared with dust shines brilliantly when it has been cleaned, so the embodied one, having seen the truth of the Self, becomes one, his purpose fulfilled, free from sorrow.
When the yogi, by the truth of the Self as if by a lamp, sees the truth of Brahman, then, knowing the God — unborn, steadfast, pure from all things — he is freed from all evils.
This God is in all the quarters. He was born first, and he is within the womb. He alone is born, and he will be born; facing all persons, he stands with faces on every side.
The God who is in fire, who is in water, who has entered the whole world, who is in plants and in trees — to that God be homage, homage.
The One who holds the net, who rules by his ruling powers, who rules all the worlds by his ruling powers — he alone is at the origin and at the coming into being. Those who know this become immortal.

Rudra is indeed One; there is no place for a second. He rules these worlds by his ruling powers; he stands facing all beings, and at the end of time, having created all worlds, the Protector withdraws them.
With eyes on every side, faces on every side, arms on every side and feet on every side, the One God, producing heaven and earth, forges them with arms and wings.
He who is the source and origin of the gods, the lord of all, Rudra, the great seer, who first gave birth to Hiranyagarbha — may he endow us with good understanding.
O Rudra, that form of yours which is auspicious, not terrible, revealing nothing evil — with that most benign form, O dweller of the mountain, look upon us.
O dweller of the mountain, the arrow that you hold in your hand to shoot — make it benign, O protector of the mountain; do not harm person or world.
Beyond this is the supreme Brahman, the vast, hidden in all beings according to their bodies, the One enveloping the whole universe. Knowing him as Lord, they become immortal.
Than whom there is nothing higher, than whom there is nothing smaller or greater, who stands alone like a tree established in heaven — by that Person all this is filled.
That which is beyond this is formless and free from suffering. Those who know this become immortal; others go only to sorrow.
Having faces, heads and necks on every side, dwelling in the cave of all beings, all-pervading — that Lord is therefore omnipresent, Shiva.
The great Lord, the Person, is the impeller of being; he brings about this most pure attainment — the ruler, the imperishable light.
The Person of the measure of a thumb, the inner Self, is ever seated in the hearts of people; he is framed by the heart, the intellect and the mind. Those who know this become immortal.
The Person has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet. Covering the earth on every side, he extended ten fingers' breadth beyond it.
The Person is all this — what has been and what is yet to be; he is also the lord of immortality, and of that which grows by food.
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads and faces everywhere, with ears everywhere in the world, he stands enveloping all.
Shining with the qualities of all the senses, yet free of all the senses; the lord and ruler of all, the refuge and friend of all.
In the city of nine gates the embodied swan flutters outside; the controller of the whole world, of all that moves and all that is still.
Without hands or feet, he moves and grasps; without eyes, he sees; without ears, he hears. He knows what is to be known, but no one knows him; they call him the primal, great Person.

Smaller than the small, greater than the great, the Self is hidden in the heart of this creature. One free from desire sees him, free from sorrow, by the grace of the Creator, and beholds his majesty and lordship.
I know this undecaying, ancient One, the Self of all, omnipresent by his pervasiveness, whose birth they deny — and the expounders of Brahman declare him eternal.

The One who, though without colour, by the union of his powers bestows many colours, hiding his purpose within; in whom the universe dissolves at the end and from whom it begins — may that God endow us with good understanding.
That indeed is Agni, that is Aditya, that is Vayu, and that is the Moon. That is the pure, that is Brahman, that is the waters, that is Prajapati.
You are woman, you are man; you are the youth and also the maiden. You, as an old man, totter along with a staff; being born, you become facing in every direction.

You are the dark-blue bird, the green one with red eyes, the one with lightning in its womb, the seasons and the seas. You exist without beginning, by your all-pervading nature, and from you all the worlds were born.
One unborn female, red, white and black, producing many offspring of like form; and one unborn male lies beside her, delighting in her, while another unborn leaves her when her enjoyment is done.
Two birds, close companions, cling to the same tree. One of them eats the sweet fruit; the other looks on without eating.
On the same tree the person sits sunk, and grieves in his helplessness, deluded. But when he sees the other, the Lord who is worshipped, and his greatness, he becomes free from sorrow.

In the imperishable syllable of the Rig Veda, in the highest heaven, on which all the gods are seated — he who does not know that, what will he do with the Rig Veda? Those who know that, they sit here together.
The metres, the sacrifices, the rites, the vows, the past, the future, and what the Vedas declare — the Maker of illusion sends forth all this from it, and in it the other is confined by illusion.
Know that Nature is illusion (maya), and the great Lord is the Maker of illusion. This whole world is pervaded by beings that are parts of him.
He who, One alone, presides over every source, in whom all this comes together and dissolves — having realised him, the lord, the bestower of boons, the adorable God, one attains this supreme peace.
He who is the source and origin of the gods, the lord of all, Rudra, the great seer — behold Hiranyagarbha being born! May he endow us with good understanding.
He who is the lord of the gods, in whom the worlds rest, who rules over this world of two-footed and four-footed beings — to what God shall we offer oblation?
Subtler than the subtle, in the midst of chaos, the creator of the universe, of many forms, the One who encompasses the universe — knowing him as Shiva, one attains supreme peace.
He alone is the guardian of the world in time, the lord of all, hidden in all beings, in whom the Brahmin sages and the gods are united; knowing him thus, one cuts the fetters of death.
Knowing Shiva, hidden in all beings, extremely subtle like the cream above clarified butter, the One who encompasses the universe, and knowing the God, one is freed from all fetters.
This God, the maker of all things, the great Self, ever seated in the hearts of people, is framed by the heart, the intellect and the mind. Those who know this become immortal.
When there is no darkness, no day nor night, neither being nor non-being — Shiva alone. That is the Imperishable, the excellent light of Savitr, and from it ancient wisdom came forth.
No one has grasped him above, or across, or in the middle. There is no likeness of him, whose name is great glory.
His form does not stand within sight; no one sees him with the eye. Those who know him thus, as dwelling in the heart, by heart and mind, become immortal.
He is unborn — thus, in fear, someone takes refuge in him. O Rudra, protect me always with your right-hand face.
Do not harm us in our children or grandchildren, in our lives, in our cattle or in our horses. Do not, O Rudra, in anger slay our heroes; bearing oblations, we call upon you always.
He who, One alone, presides over every source and over all forms and all wombs; who first bore in his knowledge the sage Kapila, born red, and beheld him as he was being born.
Spreading out one net after another in many ways, this God draws them in again in this field; having created again, the Lord, the great Self, exercises sovereignty over all.
As the sun shines, illuminating all the quarters, above, below and across, so that adorable God, the Lord, One alone, presides over all that is born of a womb.
He who, the source of the universe, ripens what has its own nature, and causes all that is to be ripened to develop; who, One alone, presides over this whole universe and assigns all the qualities.
That is hidden in the secret teaching of the Vedas, the Upanishads; Brahma knows it as the source of Brahman. The gods and sages of old who knew it became identified with it and immortal.

He who is endowed with qualities, who does works for their fruit and enjoys the results of what he has done — that being, of every form, of three qualities, following three paths, lord of the vital breaths, wanders according to his own works.

Of the measure of a thumb, like the sun in appearance, endowed with will and ego — by the quality of the intellect and the quality of the body he is seen as being of the size of the point of an awl, and yet also other.
Take the tip of a hair, divide it into a hundred parts, and each part again into a hundred; that part is to be known as the individual soul, and it is capable of infinity.
It is neither woman nor man, nor is it neuter; whatever body it takes, with that it is joined.

Through the delusions of intention, touch and sight, and through the growth and birth of the self by food and the rain of water, the embodied one successively attains forms in various places according to his deeds.
The embodied one chooses many forms, gross and subtle, according to his own qualities. By the qualities of his actions and the qualities of the self, another is also seen as the cause of their union.
Without beginning or end, in the midst of chaos, the creator of the universe, of many forms, the One who encompasses the universe — knowing that God, one is freed from all fetters.
He who is grasped by feeling, called the Bodiless, the maker of being and non-being, the auspicious, the creator of the parts — those who know that God have left the body behind.
Some sages speak of inherent nature, and others, deluded, of time. But it is the greatness of God in the world by which this wheel of Brahman is made to turn.

By him who is all-knowing, the maker of time, endowed with qualities and omniscient, this whole world is ever enveloped. Ruled by him, works proceed — earth, water, fire, air and space are to be reflected upon.
Having done that work and withdrawn again, joining in yoga with the essence of the truth — by one, by two, by three or by eight, and by time, and by the subtle qualities of the self.

He who begins works endowed with qualities and assigns all beings to their places — in their absence the work he has done is destroyed; and when the work is exhausted, he goes on, in truth, as another.

He is the beginning, the cause of the union of causes, beyond the three times, and yet seen as without parts. Having first worshipped that God, of universal form, the source of being, worthy of praise, who dwells in one's own mind —

He is beyond and other than the forms of tree, time and appearance, from whom this world of manifestation revolves. Knowing him, the bringer of righteousness, the remover of evil, the lord of fortune, as abiding in the self, the immortal, the abode of all —
He has no work to do and no organ; none is seen equal to him or greater. His supreme power is heard to be of many kinds, and his knowledge, strength and action are natural to him.
He has no master in the world, no ruler, and no mark. He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the organs; he has no begetter and no overlord.
The One God who, like a spider with its threads, covers himself by his own nature with the threads born of Pradhana — may he grant us merging in Brahman.
The One controller of the many who are inactive, who makes one seed manifold — the wise who see him dwelling in the self have eternal happiness, and no others.

The eternal among the eternals, the conscious among the conscious, the One who fulfils the desires of the many — that cause, to be reached by Sankhya and Yoga; knowing that God, one is freed from all fetters.
The sun does not shine there, nor the moon and stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire. When he shines, everything shines after him; by his light all this is illumined.
The One swan is in the midst of this world; he alone is the fire seated in the water. Only by knowing him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path to go.

He is the maker of all, the knower of all, the source of himself, the knower, the time of time, the possessor of qualities, the omniscient; the lord of Pradhana and the knower of the field, the master of the qualities, the cause of bondage and release from the cycle of existence.
He is of that nature, immortal, abiding as Lord, the knower, omnipresent, the guardian of this world, who rules this world forever; there is no other cause for ruling.
Him who first creates Brahma, and who sends forth the Vedas to him — that God, the light of the knowledge of the Self, I, desiring liberation, seek as my refuge.
Without parts, without action, tranquil, blameless, spotless, the highest bridge to immortality, like a fire that has burned up its fuel.

By the power of austerity and by the grace of God, the wise Shvetashvatara declared Brahman rightly to the ascetics of the highest order — the supreme, pure teaching, honoured by the assembly of sages.
This supreme secret in the Vedanta, taught in a former age, should not be given to one who is not tranquil, nor again to one who is not a son or a disciple.
To one who has the highest devotion to God, and as to God so to the teacher — to that great soul these matters, when told, shine forth.
To him the Grandsire replied: Know it through faith, devotion, meditation and yoga.

Those who have ascertained the meaning of the knowledge of the Vedanta, the ascetics of pure mind through the discipline of renunciation, in the worlds of Brahman, at the supreme end of time, being supremely immortal, are all liberated.

In a secluded place, seated in a comfortable posture, pure, with the body, head and neck in one straight line, standing beyond the stages of life, restraining all the senses, and bowing to one's teacher with devotion —

Meditating in the heart on the lotus, free from dust and utterly pure, and in its centre the clear, sorrowless One — the unthinkable, the unmanifest, of endless form, the auspicious, the tranquil, the immortal, the source of Brahma —

Him who is without beginning, middle or end, the One, the all-pervading, consciousness and bliss, formless, wonderful — the Supreme Lord, the master, accompanied by Uma, three-eyed, blue-throated, tranquil — having meditated on him, the sage goes to the source of beings, the witness of all, beyond darkness.
He is Brahma, he is Shiva, he is Indra; he is the Imperishable, the Supreme, the self-luminous. He alone is Vishnu, he is the vital breath, he is Time, the Fire, he is the Moon.
He alone is all that has been and all that will be, the eternal. Knowing him, one passes beyond death; there is no other path to liberation.
Making the Self the lower fire-stick and Om the upper fire-stick, by the practice of the churning of knowledge the wise man burns away sin.
That same Self, deluded by Maya and having taken a body, does everything; through the varied enjoyments of women, food, drink and the like, it in the waking state attains satisfaction.

In dream, that individual soul experiences pleasure and pain in a world of individual souls conjured up by its own Maya. In deep sleep, when everything is dissolved, overcome by darkness it attains a state of bliss.

Again, through the connection with the deeds of another birth, that same soul sleeps and awakens. The soul that plays in the three cities — from it all this manifold universe is born. In the substratum, bliss, undivided consciousness, the three cities dissolve.
That which is the supreme Brahman, the Self of all, the great abode of the universe, subtler than the subtle, eternal — that you are; you yourself are That.
That which is the enjoyable in the three states, the enjoyer, and the enjoyment — I am distinct from them: the witness, pure consciousness, the ever-auspicious Shiva.

I am indeed smaller than the smallest and likewise greater than the great; I am the manifold universe. I am the ancient, I am the Person, I am the Lord, I am the golden one; I am of the form of Shiva.
I am without hands and feet, of inconceivable power; I see without eyes, I hear without ears. I know, of secluded form, and there is no knower of me — I am ever consciousness.

I am the one to be known through the many Vedas; I am the maker of the Vedanta and the knower of the Vedas. For me there is neither merit nor sin, neither destruction nor birth; body, senses and intellect do not exist for me.
There is for me no earth, no water, no fire, no air and no space. Having thus known the nature of the Supreme Self, dwelling in the cave of the heart, without parts, without a second —

— one attains the pure nature of the Supreme Self, the witness of all, free from being and non-being. He who studies the Shatarudriya is purified by fire, is purified from drinking liquor, is purified from the murder of a Brahmin, is purified from the theft of gold, is purified from right and wrong deeds; therefore he takes refuge in the Avimukta and, standing beyond the stages of life, should always recite it, or at least once. By this he attains knowledge that destroys the ocean of worldly existence; therefore, knowing him thus, he attains the state of Kaivalya — he attains the state of Kaivalya.

Brihaspati said to Yajnavalkya: "That Kurukshetra which is the sacrificial ground of the gods and the dwelling of Brahman for all beings — the Avimukta is indeed Kurukshetra, the sacrificial ground of the gods and the dwelling of Brahman for all beings. Therefore, wherever one goes, let him think, 'This is that very Avimukta.' Indeed this is Kurukshetra, the sacrificial ground of the gods, the dwelling of Brahman for all beings. For here, when the breaths of a creature are departing, Rudra declares the saving Brahman, by which one becomes immortal and attains liberation. Therefore let one resort to the Avimukta alone; let him not abandon the Avimukta." So said Yajnavalkya.

Then Atri asked Yajnavalkya: "How shall I know this Self who is infinite and unmanifest?" Yajnavalkya said: "He is to be worshipped as the Avimukta; this Self who is infinite and unmanifest is established in the Avimukta." "In what is the Avimukta established?" "Between the Varana and the Nasi." "What is the Varana, and what is the Nasi?" "It wards off (varayati) all the faults done by the senses, therefore it is the Varana; it destroys (nashayati) all the sins done by the senses, therefore it is the Nasi." "And which is its place?" "The junction of the eyebrows and the nose — that is the junction of the heavenly world and the world beyond. Knowers of Brahman worship this junction as their twilight; the Avimukta is to be worshipped." He teaches the knowledge of the Avimukta — he who knows this thus.

Then the students of Brahman said to him: "Tell us, by what recitation is immortality gained?" Yajnavalkya said: "By the Shatarudriya; these indeed are the names of the immortal. By these one becomes immortal." So said Yajnavalkya.

Then Janaka of Videha approached Yajnavalkya and said: "Venerable one, teach me renunciation." Yajnavalkya said: "Having completed the student life, let one become a householder; having been a householder, let him become a forest-dweller; having been a forest-dweller, let him wander forth. Or otherwise, let him wander forth straight from the student life, from the household, or from the forest. Again, whether he has taken vows or not, whether he has bathed or not, or has let his fires go out — on the very day he becomes dispassionate, on that day let him wander forth. Some perform the Prajapatya sacrifice; but let him not do so — let him perform only the Agneyi, for fire is the vital breath, and he thereby makes it so. Let him perform the Traidhatavi, for the three elements are sattva, rajas and tamas. With the mantra 'This is your source, from which, born, you shone from the breath; knowing that breath, ascend, O Agni, and increase our wealth,' let him smell the fire. This vital breath is indeed the source of fire; with 'Go to the breath, svaha' he says just this. Let him bring fire from a village and have it smelt first. If he cannot find fire, let him offer in water: 'Water is indeed all the gods; to all the gods I offer, svaha.' Having offered, let him take it up and eat the oblation with clarified butter — a healthy one; this is the mantra of liberation, to be spoken in the threefold way. This is Brahman; this is to be worshipped." "So it is, venerable one," said Yajnavalkya.

Then Atri asked Yajnavalkya: "I ask you, Yajnavalkya: how is one without the sacred thread a Brahmin?" Yajnavalkya said: "This very Self is his sacred thread. Having sipped water and rinsed the mouth, this is the rule for wandering ascetics: on the path of the heroes, or in fasting, or in entering water, or entering fire, or the great departure. Then the wanderer, wearing a discoloured cloth, shaven-headed, possessing nothing, pure, free from malice, living on alms, becomes fit for oneness with Brahman. If he is ill, let him renounce in mind and speech. This is the path found by Brahman; by it the renunciate, the knower of Brahman, goes." "So it is, venerable one," said Yajnavalkya.

Among the Paramahamsas — Samvartaka, Aruni, Shvetaketu, Durvasa, Ribhu, Nidagha, Jadabharata, Dattatreya, Raivataka and others — hidden in mark, hidden in conduct, not mad yet behaving like the mad, one throws into the water, with "bhuh svaha," the triple staff, the water-pot, the sling, the bowl, the water-strainer, the topknot and the sacred thread — all of these — and seeks the Self. Bearing the form of a newborn, without knots, without possessions, well established in the path of Brahman, pure in mind, freed at the appointed time to sustain the breath, going for alms with the stomach as his bowl, equal in gain and loss, dwelling without a house in empty houses, temples, grass huts, anthills, the roots of trees, potters' sheds, fire-houses, riverbanks, mountain caves, hollows, waterfalls and open ground — striving, without possessiveness, devoted to pure meditation, established in the Self, intent on uprooting inauspicious deeds — he who gives up the body through renunciation is called a Paramahamsa; he is called a Paramahamsa.
Om. Salutation to Shiva, the teacher, whose form is being, consciousness and bliss — to the world-free, the tranquil, the support-free, the radiant.

He who, taking refuge in the Supportless, abandons all that has support, is a renunciate and a yogi, and attains the state of Kaivalya. For the sake of the peace of all evils of those ignorant beings, I shall speak, raising every question about whatever is to be known.

What is Brahman? Who is the Lord? Who is the individual soul? What is Nature? Who is the Supreme Self? Who is Brahma? Who is Vishnu? Who is Rudra? Who is Indra? Who is Yama? Who is the Sun? Who is the Moon? Who are the gods? Who are the demons? Who are the ghouls? Who are human beings? Who are women?

Who are the animals and the rest? What is the immovable? Who are the Brahmins and others? What is caste? What is action? What is non-action? What is knowledge? What is ignorance? What is pleasure? What is pain? What is heaven? What is hell? What is bondage? What is liberation? Who is to be worshipped?

Who is the disciple? Who is the learned? Who is the deluded? What is the demonic? What is austerity? What is the supreme state? What is to be accepted? What is not to be accepted? Who is the renunciate? To this he answers: Brahman. He said: that which shines as the cosmic egg, with the great principle, ego, earth, water, fire, air and space, as the form of action, knowledge and objects; the non-dual, free from all limiting adjuncts, augmented by all powers, without beginning or end, pure, auspicious, tranquil, attributeless — describable by such terms and yet indescribable — that consciousness is Brahman.
And "the Lord":

Brahman itself, resting on its own power called Nature, creates the worlds, enters them as the inner controller, and, being the ruler of the intellect and senses of Brahma and the others, is the Lord.

And "the individual soul": through name and form, by the false superimposition "I am gross" in Brahma, Vishnu, Ishana, Indra and others, it is the individual soul. That one, though single, through the divisions that form the bodies, becomes many individual souls. And "Nature": from Brahman, the power of Brahman that takes the form of the capacity for creating the manifold universe is itself Nature.

And "the Supreme Self": because it is beyond the body and the rest, Brahman itself is the Supreme Self. It is Brahma, it is Vishnu, it is Indra, it is Yama, it is the Sun, it is the Moon; they are the gods, they are the demons, they are the ghouls, they are human beings, they are women, they are animals and the rest, that is the immovable, they are Brahmins and others. All this is indeed Brahman; there is no multiplicity here at all.

And "caste": not of skin, not of blood, not of flesh, nor of bone is the Self's caste; caste is imagined for practical dealings. And "action": action performed through the acting senses, done with the settled thought "I act" in relation to the Self — that alone is action. And "non-action": that which binds through the sense of doing and enjoying, the cause of birth and the rest, the seeking of fruit in regular and occasional sacrifices, vows, austerities, gifts and the like — that is non-action.

And "knowledge": by control of body and senses, service to a true teacher, hearing, reflection and deep contemplation, the direct experience that the nature of the seer and the seen, dwelling within all and equal in all — like pots and cloths and the like — is unchanging, and that without consciousness there is nothing among changing things: that is knowledge.

And "ignorance": like the delusion of a snake in a rope, the imagined knowledge, in the non-dual, all-pervading Brahman that is all, of the divisions of gods, animals, men, immovables, women, men, castes and stages of life, bondage, liberation and limiting adjuncts as different selves — that is ignorance. And "pleasure": having known the nature of being, consciousness and bliss, the state that is of the nature of bliss — that alone is pleasure.

Pain: intention directed to objects, which is not-Self in form, is itself pain. "Heaven": the company of the good is heaven. "Hell": the company of people attached to the worldly objects of the untrue is itself hell. "Bondage": the intention "I was born" arising from beginningless ignorance and habit is bondage.

The intention of possessiveness about father, mother, siblings, wife, children, house, garden and field — the intention that veils worldly existence — is bondage. The intention of ego in being the doer and so on is bondage. The intention of desire for the accomplishment of the eight powers, beginning with the power of becoming minute, is bondage. The intention of desire in the worship of gods and men is bondage. The intention of the eight-limbed yoga beginning with restraint is bondage.

The intention of the duties and rites of caste and stage of life is bondage. The intention of the qualities of command, fear, doubt and the self is bondage. The knowledge arising from the rules of sacrifice, vow, austerity and gift is bondage. The intention that merely awaits liberation is bondage. Whatever arises merely as intention is bondage. And "liberation": from discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal, the destruction of the bond of possessiveness for all fields, and of the pleasures and pains of impermanent worldly life, is liberation.

And "the one to be worshipped": the teacher, who leads to Brahman as consciousness abiding in all bodies, is to be worshipped. And "the disciple": one in whom the world has been destroyed by knowledge, who has entered into it, and in whom only Brahman remains as knowledge — he alone is the disciple. And "the learned": one who knows his own inner awareness abiding within all. And "the deluded": one who has climbed onto the notion of ego in being the doer and so on.

And "the demonic": the austerity which, through the desire for the lordship of Brahma, Vishnu, Ishana, Indra and others, torments the inner self by fasting, recitation and fire-offerings, and which depends on intense attachment, hatred, violence and pride, is demonic. And "austerity": through the fire of direct knowledge that Brahman is true and the world false, the burning of the seed of the intention of desire for the lordship of Brahma and others — that is austerity.

And "the supreme state": beyond breath, senses and the qualities of the inner organ, the eternally free abode of Brahman, made of being, consciousness and bliss, is the supreme state. "What is to be accepted": the nature of pure consciousness, free from the limitations of place, time and object, is to be accepted. "What is not to be accepted": the thought that the world, the object of the illusory intellect and senses and different from one's own nature, is real — that is not to be accepted.

And "the renunciate": having given up all duties, without possessiveness and without ego, having taken refuge in the chosen Brahman, from the knowledge that comes by experiencing the meaning of the great sayings — "That thou art," "I am Brahman," "All this is indeed Brahman; there is no multiplicity here at all" — having resolved "I am Brahman itself," the ascetic moves about independent through non-dual absorption; he is the renunciate, he is liberated, he is worthy of worship, he is the yogi, he is the Paramahamsa, he is the Avadhuta, he is the Brahmin.

Whoever studies this Niralamba Upanishad by the grace of the teacher becomes purified by fire, becomes purified by air; he does not return again, he does not return again; he is not born again, he is not born again. Thus the Upanishad.
Om. That is full; this is full; from the full the full arises. Taking the full from the full, the full alone remains.
